Objectives: Weed treatments to prevent the spread of invasive and noxious weed species, including invasive\r\nannual grasses (medusahead rye and cheatgrass)
Planned_Implementation: The SW AT crew will make site visits, prioritizing sites with high potential for noxious weed establishment, and treat any small establishing populations with the appropriate approved herbicides. Application of all herbicides will follow given products directions for appropriate application rates (specific to species being targeted). All located populations of noxious\r\nweeds will be recorded (GPS'd and logged into a database) to track effectiveness (see below).
Actual_Implementation:
During the FY2015 field season, 65,453 acres of the Riley Field fire
were sprayed with an aerial application of Imazapic at 6oz/acre in
order to suppress the infestation of medusahead rye, which was,
and is, abundant within the fire perimeter as well as outside. A
buffer was used to treat areas outside the fire perimeter in order
to prevent reinfestation of the burned area after treatment.
Unfortunately, the initial treatment was only moderately
successful due to weather variables requiring a second treatment
during the FY16 field season. Between 2016 and 2017, an
additional 60,000 were treated with imazapic to attempt to
suppress the medusahead rye.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
This fire was originally on the former three-year plan format. Because policy at that time
prohibited weed treatments for ES treatment of invasive annual grasses, this plan was not fully
successful. Having to postpone weed treatments due to on-the-ground conditions of heavy
medusahead infestations negated most drill seeding opportunities and any success we may
have had in combating the infestation and establishing desirable vegetation. Due to this, we
opted to proceed under the established three-year plan rather than extend to five years under
the current plan structure.
We were able to utilize other funds outside of ESR to do our initial weed treatments necessary
the first fall after the fire (2015); however, those treatments were not as successful as hoped
and were reapplied in 2016 in the areas deemed most likely to recover naturally due to
remnant native and desirable perennial bunchgrasses and forbs.
The Environmental Assessment for the Riley Field ESR Plan was included with the combined
Buzzard Complex EA. This EA was completed jointly between the Burns and Vale Districts which
left both Districts vulnerable to appeal and litigation on a larger scale. Additionally, because of
differing resource priorities, the EA, with signed FONSI and DR, was more confusing than most
ESR EAs. I would recommend NOT doing joint ESR EAs or ESR Plans for this reason.
As stated above, in 2014 weed treatments for invasive annual grasses were not an Emergency
Stabilization priority and considered a pre-existing condition, which lead to less funding for the
treatments in, BAR. The Riley Field fire occurred in one of the most heavily infested
medusahead areas on the Burns District. The best time to treat this invasive annual grass, based
on research by the Burns USDA-ARS (research plots which were actually burned in the fire), is
immediately following fire, before the soil seed bank has a chance to germinate in the fall.
Unfortunately, we were unable to conduct these treatments in a timely fashion we determined
that we’d missed the windows for both aerial and drill seeding within most of designated
treatment areas.
Field season 2016 left us with no extra staff to conduct monitoring; however, in one year, and a
drought year, there were no significant changes in vegetation from 2015.

Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives:
The fire caused mortality of desirable perennial plants which created new open habitats for noxious weeds to expand into. Noxious weed infestations provide unstable and poor quality habitat for sagebrush steppe obligate plant and wildlife species. The objectives of noxious weed treatment and inventory is to continue treating previously known infestation sites and identify the spread of noxious and invasive weeds in the burned area. There are identified weeds present in the burned area and if not treated, are expected to increase due to the removal of existing vegetation by the Saddle Draw Fire. Past treatments in the area have been relatively successful, by continuing to inventory and treat infestation known and new
sites the frequency of noxious weeds is expected to be reduced.
In the 2012 Long Draw fire, for example, Scotch thistle rosettes were still green two weeks after the ignition date of the fire and dead looking stalks were sprouting new limbs with all buds and rush skeletonweed had resprouted and was blooming within eight weeks of being burned over by fire. Disturbances caused by fireline construction and other control
actions create niches where weeds can readily establish and dominate.
Planned_Implementation:
Weed treatments will be focused on known sites and limiting establishment of new sites in the fire area. Scotch thistle, bull thistle, Canada thistle, Russian knapweed, spotted knapweed, diffuse knapweed, perennial pepperweed, whitetop species, and halogeton are located within the burn area. Dalmatian toadflax has been identified and treated in the Hwy.
78 corridor at the west edge of the fire. Rush skeletonweed (Chondrilla juncea) was reported, but not confirmed, during fire control activities. Small populations of invasive and/or noxious annual grasses have been identified within native, perennial plant communities. These existing small populations can out-compete fire-stressed natives and become the dominant vegetation following wildfires.
Noxious weeds and invasive plants are most abundant along roads in the fire area. Thus, weed treatments will be focused along roads. Disturbances along roads are natural conduits for noxious and invasive weeds and grasses. They are easily spread along existing roads and especially dozer and grader lines, eventually making their way into the interior rangeland.
Noxious weed inventory and treatment would help to control existing populations, help discover new populations, and reduce the risk of further establishment of noxious weeds. Every Standard Operating Procedure that are part of our H-9011, 9015, 9220 manuals and in Appendix A of OR Veg EIS ROD, as well as safety and range manuals, that pertain to weed treatment and management will be adhered to. The Weed Program is directed to consider every one for every site, except maybe the aerial ones if we are doing ground treatments and vice versa.
Aerial invasive grass treatments with imazapic, chlorsulfuron or clopyralid along existing roads as well as identified blocks within the burned area would be done in the first proper biological window, preferably fall of 2014, to curtail its expansion. Ground treatment on the known sites of noxious weeds would occur within first proper biological/environmental
windows, following the fire (FY15). In years two (FY 2016) and three (FY 2017), the noxious and invasive weeds/grasses inventory, monitoring, and treatment would be included as a rehabilitation treatment. The Vale District is currently working on the NEPA to authorize the use of imazapic, chlorsulfuron or clopyralid.
There are currently only four herbicides that the BLM is authorized to use in Oregon. Of those, picloram, 2,4-D and dicamba or a combination of the three will be used on the broad leaved species on upland sites. In riparian areas, there can be no picloram used, so that leaves 2,4-D and dicamba according to label; near water, we have to resort to glyphosate.
Rates of application from OR Veg EIS ROD, Table 1, pg 11, maximum: 2,4-D 1.9 lbs/ac; dicamba 3 lbs/ac; glyphosate 7 lbs/ac; picloram 1 lb/ac. Chemical treatments would be applied following Best Management Practices (BMPs) and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) as outlined in the Record of Decision (ROD) for Vegetation Treatments Using Herbicides on BLM Lands in Oregon (2010). Selected herbicide, rates, timing, etc., will vary for each site and each treated species and will be
applied according to individual label instructions. Imazapic, chlorsulfuron or clopyralid would be applied using the best science available, utilizing Agricultural Research Service (ARS) knowledge, research and documentation; working with chemical representatives familiar with local treatments; and, according to label.
Chemical treatment of invasive grasses and noxious weed populations, closing the area to livestock and seeding competitive perennial grasses would reduce the likelihood of their spread to new unoccupied areas and help to re-establish higher quality vegetation. Noxious weeds also threaten adjacent private range and agricultural lands. Furthermore, noxious
weed infestations have little to no value to wildlife, wild horses or livestock and are considered one of the greatest threats to loss of sage grouse habitat.
Actual_Implementation:
The fire area was inventoried in the fall of 2014 and throughout the
summer of 2015. Noxious weeds were treated with Imazapic along
both sides of Crowley-Riverside road and several other areas of
high infestation

Based on adaptive management field assessments (See Part 6, S 13) and confirmed by
preliminary data obtained during USGS monitoring, the following modifications were made
regarding aerial Imazapic applications
3,800 acres of Succor Creek allotment pastures 2, 3 and 4, and Pasture 1 of the Jackson Creek
allotment were retreated because first herbicide application did not meet objectives and it was
determined a second treatment was needed prior to the drill seeding. (See maps Appendix D, S5
FY16).
• 8,060 acres of the areas drill seeded in fall of 2015 were treated in the Strodes Basin,
Sands Basin, Rockville, Blackstock Springs, Juniper Spring, Stateline, Jackson Creek,
Joint, and Reynolds Creek allotments.
• Approximately 8,900 acres drill seeded in 2015 were not treated with aerial herbicide in
2016; either drill seedings were progressing adequately without herbicide such that the
treatment was not deemed necessary (Rockville 1, portions of Blackstock Springs 1,
Juniper Spring 2, 3 and portions of 4, Stateline 1, Shares Basin 2, 6), or the annual grass
cover was deemed too high for aerial herbicide to be successful (Juniper Spring 1 and
Sands Basin 4).
• 10,580 acres of the areas aerially seeded with grasses in winter of2016 were treated in
the Blackstock Springs, Bush Ranch FFR, Jackson Creek, Juniper Spring, Reynolds
Creek, Rockville, Stanford FFR, Stateline, and Succor Creek allotments.
• 10,540 acres on steeper hillsides were treated to reduce annual invasive, release existing
perennials, and open up areas to seed sagebrush. Alkali-Wildcat, Strodes Basin, Sands
Basin, Shares Basin Juniper Spring, Blackstock Spring, Jackson Creek and Succor Creek
allotments.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2020 the foliar cover objective for the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment was met; mean foliar cover of annual invasive grasses for across all allotments and pastures was 16.2% (Table 8-51). Pastures with greater than 20% annual invasive grass foliar cover had less than 10% large-statured perennial grass foliar cover. In pastures with higher annual invasive grasses, Sandberg bluegrass cover was also below 10%. The one plot within the Wilson pasture of Reynolds Creek Allotment had the highest annual invasive grass foliar cover with 92. 8%, this pasture also had no deep-rooted perennial grasses or Sandberg bluegrass. Within all plots in 2020 in the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment area, perennial bunchgrass cover was 17.6%, Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover was 8.6%, perennial forb cover was 2.1%, and shrub cover was 2.0%.
In 2020 the foliar cover objective for the Fall 2016 Herbicide Treatment was met; mean foliar cover of annual invasive grasses for across all allotments and pastures was 17.2% (Table 8-52). Similar to the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment, pastures with higher annual invasive grass cover tended to have lower deep rooter perennial grass and Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover, though the effect was not as pronounced as for the spring treatment. Within all plots in 2020 in the Fall 2016 Herbicide Treatment area, perennial bunchgrass foliar cover was 21.0%, Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover was 12.2%, perennial forb cover was 3.6%, and shrub cover was 2.1%.
///
Monitoring Report 2019: 1. Foliar cover of invasive annual grasses is an average of less than or equal to 20%.
This treatment objective was met in 2019; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 12.54, varying from 3.04 to 16.25% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.93% varying from 0 to 32.66% in 2018 (Table 8-46).
In 2018 this treatment objective was met; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 8.06, varying from 0.51 to 14.02% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.70% varying from 0 to 35.13% in 2018 (Table 8-46). Pastures that in 2017 had high invasive annual grass cover were not monitored in 2018 as the objectives were not met in these areas and were not likely to meet.
In 2017 the highest annual grass foliar cover was found in Pasture 3 (37%) of Elephant Butte, Pasture 2 (77%) and Pasture 3 (61%) of Hardtrigger, and Pasture 1 (65%) of Reynolds Creek. The herbicide treatment areas within these pastures were along proposed fuel breaks at elevations below 2,600 ft; areas dominated by annual grasses before the fire. These areas also experienced large amounts of annual grass germination prior to the herbicide treatment. This likely resulted in the low amount of annual grass control that was observed in 2016. The remaining areas treated with herbicide were above 3,200 ft elevation. Annual grass foliar cover in these pastures ranged from 0.51% in Pasture 4 of Hardtrigger, which is above 4,200 ft elevation, to 28% in Pasture 2 of Succor Creek, an area that is above 4,500 feet elevation but had high cheatgrass and medusahead cover before the Soda fire.
Based on adaptive management field assessments (Appendix B) that were confirmed by preliminary data obtained from this monitoring, portions of Pastures 2, 3 and 4 of the Succor Creek allotment, and Pasture 1 of the Jackson Creek allotment were retreated with herbicide to control annual grasses during the early fall of 2016 (8-46). These areas were chosen for re-treatment, because the spring herbicide treatment appeared to be ineffective, and they also had adequate densities of perennials on site to compete with annuals or they were scheduled for drill seeding to establish adequate densities of perennials. Areas dominated by invasive annual grasses, such as those mentioned along the proposed fuel break routes, were not considered for re-treatment with aerial herbicide.
When herbicide treatment areas were re-visited in 2017 it was observed that some of the areas that appeared to be failures were now showing clear signs of annual grass suppression. The most apparent example was along the fuel breaks within Pastures 2 and 3 of the Hardtrigger allotment. Treated areas had shown no signs of cheatgrass suppression in 2016, but suppression was very apparent in 2017. It is likely that the cheatgrass that had germinated prior to the herbicide application in spring 2016 was too developed to be suppressed by imazapic. However, the imazapic remained active in the soil and was clearly suppressing germination in 2017. It is possible that Jackson Creek Pasture 1 would have exhibit the “delayed control” however, it was re-treated with imazapic in fall 2016 to ensure a clean seedbed prior to drill seeding in fall 2017.
////
There were several important findings during inventory the first year post-fire:
Several new small infestations ( <0.1 acre) of leafy spurge were found within a 250 acre area near
Cow Creek. These sites were immediately treated and will continue to be monitored. No other
locations of leafy spurge are known to occur. No new invaders (new to the area noxious weed
species) were detected in the first year. Inventory provided a baseline of data for post-fire
potential spread of noxious weeds.
The majority of the rush skeletonweed chemical treatments occurred west of Highway 95 toward
the state line. Isolated plants were scattered south of Highway 78. Scotch thistle patches were
associated with ponds and springs. Perennial pepperweed was noted in Dry and Sage Creek
drainages. Whitetop was found east of Highway 95 from mile marker 3-7 and in the Reynolds
Creek area. Leafy spurge was noted east of Highway 95 near Succor Creek. Diffuse knapweed
was found at the old gravel pit near Highway 95 at mile marker 7 and Russian knapweed was
found at the bottom of the Poison Creek grade.
Re-inventory and monitoring completed throughout 2017 showed chemical treatments completed
in 2015 and 2016 were effective in most locations especially on small, new infestations.
Herbicide efficacy is a function of timing and environmental conditions. Many treatments were
very effective at controlling that year's growth however the large amount of moisture during the
fall, winter and spring led to ideal growing conditions for some species, especially plants that
germinated in the fall or the spring from an established "seed bank" like diffuse knapweed and
scotch thistle. This led to a significant increase in the number of plants especially in areas
where relatively few plants had been observed before. These ideal growing conditions were also
very favorable for deep rooted perennial species such as whitetop, perennial pepperweed and
Russian knapweed. Overall, chemical treatment has been very effective however many
infestations still persist and will need continued treatment to maintain control.

Following the all 2016 herbicide application the medusahead was controlled resulting in areas of bare ground.

S5/R5 Inventory and Chemical Treatment-Noxious and Invasive Weeds.
Noxious weeds are present in the burned area. Noxious weeds are now recognized worldwide as posing threats to
biological diversity, second only to direct habitat loss and fragmentation. Noxious weeds are known to alter
ecosystem functions such as nutrient cycles, hydrology, and wildfire frequency; out-compete and exclude native
plants and animals; and to hybridize with native species. The presence and abundance of noxious weeds in an
ecosystem is highly dynamic subject to changes in the local environment (Whitson, T.D., et al. 1992, Cal-Ipc,
2007). All natural communities are susceptible to invasion by noxious weeds.

Objectives: Aerial Herbicide Application Fall 2015, Winter 2016 (FY16) Boise BLM.\r\n1. Foliar cover of invasive annual grasses is an average of less than or equal to 20%.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerially apply approximately 22,305 acres of the herbicide imazapic at a rate of 6 ounces per acre in the
fall of 2015 on areas suitable for drill seeding. Imazapic is a pre-emergent herbicide that is partially
selective to annual grass species and will be used as a seedbed preparation for subsequent drill seeding
treatments. Imazapic has been shown to negatively impact some established perennial grasses and forbs, as
well as sagebrush germination. Allowing sites to remain fallow for a year following the herbicide
treatment will be necessary to allow for the establishment of desired seeded species. These areas will be
drill seeded in the fall of 2016.
Actual_Implementation:
The aerial herbicide application contract was modified and the period of performance shifted to
spring 2016. Spring application was to coincide with the early emergence of cheatgrass and
medusahead rye and during the dormant season of existing perennial vegetation.
The remaining 21,798 acres were treated in the spring of 2016 as soon as conditions allowed.
Work on the contract re-commenced February 16, 2016. Temperatures during herbicide
application ranged from 35\xb0 to 65\xb0 F, clear visibility, with variable wind. The contract was
completed March 3, 2016.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Report 2020: In 2020 the foliar cover objective for the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment was met; mean foliar cover of annual invasive grasses for across all allotments and pastures was 16.2% (Table 8-51). Pastures with greater than 20% annual invasive grass foliar cover had less than 10% large-statured perennial grass foliar cover. In pastures with higher annual invasive grasses, Sandberg bluegrass cover was also below 10%. The one plot within the Wilson pasture of Reynolds Creek Allotment had the highest annual invasive grass foliar cover with 92. 8%, this pasture also had no deep-rooted perennial grasses or Sandberg bluegrass. Within all plots in 2020 in the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment area, perennial bunchgrass cover was 17.6%, Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover was 8.6%, perennial forb cover was 2.1%, and shrub cover was 2.0%.

Monitoring Report 2019: 1. Foliar cover of invasive annual grasses is an average of less than or equal to 20%.
This treatment objective was met in 2019; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 12.54, varying from 3.04 to 16.25% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.93% varying from 0 to 32.66% in 2018 (Table 8-46).
In 2018 this treatment objective was met; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 8.06, varying from 0.51 to 14.02% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.70% varying from 0 to 35.13% in 2018 (Table 8-46). Pastures that in 2017 had high invasive annual grass cover were not monitored in 2018 as the objectives were not met in these areas and were not likely to meet.
In 2017 the highest annual grass foliar cover was found in Pasture 3 (37%) of Elephant Butte, Pasture 2 (77%) and Pasture 3 (61%) of Hardtrigger, and Pasture 1 (65%) of Reynolds Creek. The herbicide treatment areas within these pastures were along proposed fuel breaks at elevations below 2,600 ft; areas dominated by annual grasses before the fire. These areas also experienced large amounts of annual grass germination prior to the herbicide treatment. This likely resulted in the low amount of annual grass control that was observed in 2016. The remaining areas treated with herbicide were above 3,200 ft elevation. Annual grass foliar cover in these pastures ranged from 0.51% in Pasture 4 of Hardtrigger, which is above 4,200 ft elevation, to 28% in Pasture 2 of Succor Creek, an area that is above 4,500 feet elevation but had high cheatgrass and medusahead cover before the Soda fire.
Based on adaptive management field assessments (Appendix B) that were confirmed by preliminary data obtained from this monitoring, portions of Pastures 2, 3 and 4 of the Succor Creek allotment, and Pasture 1 of the Jackson Creek allotment were retreated with herbicide to control annual grasses during the early fall of 2016 (8-46). These areas were chosen for re-treatment, because the spring herbicide treatment appeared to be ineffective, and they also had adequate densities of perennials on site to compete with annuals or they were scheduled for drill seeding to establish adequate densities of perennials. Areas dominated by invasive annual grasses, such as those mentioned along the proposed fuel break routes, were not considered for re-treatment with aerial herbicide.
When herbicide treatment areas were re-visited in 2017 it was observed that some of the areas that appeared to be failures were now showing clear signs of annual grass suppression. The most apparent example was along the fuel breaks within Pastures 2 and 3 of the Hardtrigger allotment. Treated areas had shown no signs of cheatgrass suppression in 2016, but suppression was very apparent in 2017. It is likely that the cheatgrass that had germinated prior to the herbicide application in spring 2016 was too developed to be suppressed by imazapic. However, the imazapic remained active in the soil and was clearly suppressing germination in 2017. It is possible that Jackson Creek Pasture 1 would have exhibit the “delayed control” however, it was re-treated with imazapic in fall 2016 to ensure a clean seedbed prior to drill seeding in fall 2017.

1. There were several important findings during inventory the first year post-fire:
Several new small infestations ( <0.1 acre) of leafy spurge were found within a 250 acre area near
Cow Creek. These sites were immediately treated and will continue to be monitored. No other
locations of leafy spurge are known to occur. No new invaders (new to the area noxious weed
species) were detected in the first year. Inventory provided a baseline of data for post-fire
potential spread of noxious weeds.
The majority of the rush skeletonweed chemical treatments occurred west of Highway 95 toward
the state line. Isolated plants were scattered south of Highway 78. Scotch thistle patches were
associated with ponds and springs. Perennial pepperweed was noted in Dry and Sage Creek
drainages. Whitetop was found east of Highway 95 from mile marker 3-7 and in the Reynolds
Creek area. Leafy spurge was noted east of Highway 95 near Succor Creek. Diffuse knapweed
was found at the old gravel pit near Highway 95 at mile marker 7 and Russian knapweed was
found at the bottom of the Poison Creek grade.
Re-inventory and monitoring completed throughout 2017 showed chemical treatments completed
in 2015 and 2016 were effective in most locations especially on small, new infestations.
Herbicide efficacy is a function of timing and environmental conditions. Many treatments were
very effective at controlling that year's growth however the large amount of moisture during the
fall, winter and spring led to ideal growing conditions for some species, especially plants that
germinated in the fall or the spring from an established "seed bank" like diffuse knapweed and
scotch thistle. This led to a significant increase in the number of plants especially in areas
where relatively few plants had been observed before. These ideal growing conditions were also
very favorable for deep rooted perennial species such as whitetop, perennial pepperweed and
Russian knapweed. Overall, chemical treatment has been very effective however many
infestations still persist and will need continued treatment to maintain control.

Planned_Implementation:
On-the-ground inspections of perennial grass mortality indicate that desirable
perennial bunchgrasses in units 4 and 7 were lost, and planting non-native desirable
bunchgrasses is a reasonable treatment to keep invasive species from filling the
vacuum. The objective of seeding Drill Seeding Units 4 and 7 early post fire is to
give the seedings the opportunity to take advantage of the nutrient release post fire,
and maximize the establishment of the seedings. If the seeding is established, the
need for herbicide application should be reduced because there will be an
established stand of perennial bunchgrasses to resist invasion by annual
grasses. Further complicating the sequence event is the inability to apply herbicide
in the fall of 2017 due to contracting and contractor limitations. An alternate
sequence of herbicide application was considered, which was to wait to apply
herbicide in the fall of 2018. There is concern, due the severity of the fire in Units 4
and 7, that waiting to spray in fall of 2018 and seeding in 2020 leaves the
sites vulnerable for an extended period of time and could create a more difficult
situation to get desirable vegetation established within the BAR funding
window. That is the rationale for seeding first, monitoring establishment of seeded
species, and then applying herbicide if invasive species threaten treatment success.
However, if the drill seeding in Units 4 and 7 does not establish, based on
monitoring results, the fall back use of herbicide to suppress invasive grasses will
be implemented. Current protocol is to use a contractor to treat 100 percent of
the 6,038 acres that are ground seeded with imazapic at a rate of 6 ounces per acre
if survey and monitoring information demonstrate the need. If there are areas that
do not need treatment, (based on monitoring and Early Detection Rapid Response
(EDRR) Crew work) they will be removed from the treatment plan and treated
acres will be reduced. This potential initial herbicide application, which will be
done by fixed wing aircraft, will target newly germinating plants in order to
suppress the spread of cheatgrass while not impacting the seeded species and
existing, naturally recovering native vegetation (mostly forbs ).
In the following years 3-5 (2020-2022), if monitoring indicates that large areas
outside of the seed units are becoming dominated by cheatgrass, they will be
treated by a broadcast application of the most appropriate approved herbicide. For
planning purposes, it is estimated that these treatments could be needed on up
to approximately 50 percent of the acres within the fire perimeter in year 3, on 25
percent in year 4, and on 15 percent in year 5. These treatments, if monitoring
shows they are necessary, will occur by fixed wing aircraft because there is little
topographic variation. The Bums District has had success using aerial applications
in the past on both fire rehabilitation and other landscape scale projects. See the
Integrated Invasive Plant Management for the Bums District Revised
Environmental Assessment (EA) (DOI-BLM-B000-2011-0041-EA) in Appendix B
for the potential herbicides and application rates for specific weed species.
In the first 3 years following the fire, an increased presence with the Strategic
Weed Attack Team (SWAT) will be necessary to ensure no new weed sources
occur due to suppression efforts; this early detection will allow us to ensure any
weed sites that occur throughout the area of the fire will remain small and not
become established. Additionally, EDRR will continue to be used to survey and
treat any new weed sites to prevent their establishment and expansion within the
fire perimeter. EDRR will include survey and treatment of small sites or patches of
noxious and/or invasive weeds and will, in addition, document any large
infestations to be treated at a later date by either ground or aerial contractors. All
sites will be entered into the National Invasive Species Information Management
System (NISIMS).

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Burns District Bureau of Land Management is proposing to implement the Emergency Stabilization and Burned Area Rehabilitation (ES & R) Plan for the Desert Meadows Fire. The Desert Meadows Fire burned 2,100 acres within the No Livestock Grazing Area of the Steens Mountain Wilderness (see map ). The fire started on a slight slope and then burned up a steep mountain side between Little Blitzen River and Dry Creek. The fire burned in such a manner as to leave a mosaic pattern of live and unburned vegetation within the burn perimeter. Directly under some juniper trees, the fire burned at high intensity resulting in black and white ash covering the soil surface. The fire killed some western juniper and removed above ground portions of sagebrush. Perennial grasses and forbs were also burned to the soil surface. The Desert Meadows Fire was contained and controlled on September 15, 2011. The fire burned near the mouth of the Little Blitzen Canyon. The fire did not burn in the Little Blitzon River riparian area. The closest the fire came to the river was 200 yards. Medusahead rye, Canada thistle and bull thistle noxious weed species are present and expanding throughout the Steens Mountain Wilderness. It is likely that these noxious weeds will establish in the burned area and outcompete the native perianal vegetation. 

Purpose and Need

The disturbance from the Desert Meadows Fire could provide opportunities for the expansion of weed species including Medusahead rye, Canada thistle and bull thistle within the burn area. Hand seeding and spraying herbicide will help reduce the likelihood of noxious weeds establishing as well as the following: 

a.	Stabilize soils after the first growing season and reduce the potential for accelerated soil erosion associated with invasive annual grass communities.
b.	Reduce the likelihood of these areas experiencing a reduced fire return interval associated with invasive annual grass communities.
c.	Promote reestablishment of other native vegetation not seeded such as Wyoming big sagebrush.

Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives: Establish perennial dominated plant communities that will help stabilize soils, out-compete noxious weeds and invasive species.
Planned_Implementation: 2,175-acre aerial application of Imazapic targeting cheatgrass and medusahead could occur
Actual_Implementation: 8 ounces of Imazapic per acre with 5 gallons water per acre were applied 9/23/21 - 9/24/21 on 2,091 acres of BLM lands and 637 acres of IDL lands. Funding was obligated through cost savings of other FY21 ESR funds.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2023 invasive annual grasses and forbs were present throughout the fire as imazapic would no longer be present in enough quantity to suppress seed germination.
Perennial bunchgrasses were Site assessments were conducted, and photos were re-taken at three monitoring plots in 2022. The herbicide application was effective though some striping, areas where herbicide was not as effective and medusahead plants and litter remain, are visible on hillslopes (photos below). Perennial grasses (bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail and Sandberg bluegrass) across the treated area were healthy and did not show impacts from the herbicide application.

Quantitative and qualitative monitoring for cover and density of invasive annual grasses was conducted in the burned area in June 2021 in two monitoring plots. Density of invasive annual grasses was 681 plants per meter squared in the plots. Disbursement outside of plot areas was varied. Additionally, medusahead rye and cheatgrass surrounds most of the burn area so treatment with imazapic within the fire perimeter was warranted to prevent further infestation.
